title: Jeremiah 2:29–37
context: The LORD still speaks through Jeremiah, now asking why the people will contend with him when they have all transgressed. Their children have been struck in vain; they received no correction, and their own sword has devoured their prophets like a destroying lion. A generation is told to consider the LORD’s word: has the LORD been a wilderness to Israel, or a land of thick darkness, that they should say they have broken loose and will come no more? A virgin does not forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire, yet the people have forgotten the LORD for days without number. They prepare their way to seek love, and have even taught the wicked women their ways—language of practiced unfaithfulness that should be read soberly, as a charge of going after others, not as a graphic scene. Blood of the souls of the innocent poor is found in their skirts; those poor were not found breaking in. The people still say they are innocent, and that the LORD’s anger has turned away; they will be judged because they say they have not sinned. They go about to change their ways, and will be ashamed of Egypt as they were of Assyria, leaving with their hands on their head; the LORD has rejected those in whom they trust, and they will not prosper with them. The speaker throughout is the LORD, with the people’s claims quoted inside the speech. The unit remains an indictment and a warning, not a finished system, and not a cue to rearrange later chapters.

verses.text: “Why will you contend with me? You all have transgressed against me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Why will you contend with me? You all have transgressed against me,” says the LORD. The people are the ones who have a case to answer, not the LORD. The charge is universal in the address: “You all have transgressed against me,” The contention they offer is turned back on them.

Arminian readers hear a real question to people who are arguing with God while being themselves the transgressors. The “all” names a shared guilt they can still be called to face.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “Why will you contend with me?” as the LORD’s rebuke of a people who bring a case while having all transgressed against him. The guilt is theirs, and the contention does not stand.

Shared ground: the people have transgressed, and their contention with the LORD is misplaced. There is no party contrast over the question itself.

verses.text: “I have struck your children in vain. They received no correction. Your own sword has devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I have struck your children in vain. They received no correction. Your own sword has devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion.” Blows meant as correction have not been received, and the people have used their own sword against the prophets, as a lion destroys. The verse does not name those prophets, and a list should not be invented.

Arminian readers take the “in vain” as a grievous fact: correction was given and was not received, a refusal, and the killing of prophets is their own doing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear strikes that did not yield correction, and a sword at home that has devoured the prophets. The LORD records both the wasted blows and the violence against his messengers.

Both traditions share the charge. The lion image describes that violence, and it needs no further story beyond what the verse says.

verses.text: Generation, consider the LORD’s word. Have I been a wilderness to Israel? Or a land of thick darkness? Why do my people say, ‘We have broken loose. We will come to you no more’?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Generation, consider the LORD’s word. Have I been a wilderness to Israel? Or a land of thick darkness? Why do my people say, ‘We have broken loose. We will come to you no more’?” The LORD asks whether he has been barren or dark to them, that they should break loose and refuse to come. The quoted saying is their own resolve to stay away.

Arminian readers hear a sincere question and a real refusal. The LORD has not been a wilderness to them, and “We will come to you no more” is a chosen breaking loose, not a conclusion forced by any failure in him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the questions as the LORD’s vindication of his own care, and the quoted words as the people’s declared independence. They have broken loose and will come no more, though he has not been a wilderness or a land of thick darkness to them.

Shared ground: the fault is not in the LORD’s dealing. The people’s saying is the evidence this verse puts forward.

verses.text: “Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me for days without number.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Can a virgin forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me for days without number.” The comparison is simple and is kept sober: a bride does not forget her attire, but the people have forgotten the LORD for countless days. The marriage image again names devotion and its loss, not a scene to describe in physical detail.

Arminian readers hear a forgetfulness that is culpable precisely because it is so unnatural. The days without number are their own long leaving, not a momentary lapse they could not help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the comparison as the LORD’s: what a bride would not forget, his people have forgotten, and the forgetting has lasted for days without number.

Both traditions share the charge and the image. It should be read as forgotten covenant love, without graphic expansion.

verses.text: How well you prepare your way to seek love! Therefore you have even taught the wicked women your ways.
verses.arminianNotes:
“How well you prepare your way to seek love! Therefore you have even taught the wicked women your ways.” The seeking of love, and the teaching of wicked women, is again the language of practiced unfaithfulness. It may picture idolatry, or a social charge, or both; the exact force can be hedged. In any case the charge is stated soberly: the people are skilled in going after others, and have even become teachers of those ways, not subjects for graphic retelling.

Arminian readers take the prepared way as a willing skill. They have arranged their path to seek love, and the teaching named here is their own furthering of that path.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same “How well you prepare your way to seek love” as the LORD’s exposure of a practiced pursuit, so practiced that they have taught others. The line is a charge of skill in unfaithfulness, to be left in that restrained sense.

Shared ground: the seeking and the teaching are condemned. The verse is not a fork, and it should not be handled as a graphic scene.

verses.text: Also the blood of the souls of the innocent poor is found in your skirts. You didn’t find them breaking in, but it is because of all these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Also the blood of the souls of the innocent poor is found in your skirts. You didn’t find them breaking in, but it is because of all these things.” Beside the unfaithfulness already named, there is blood of the innocent poor. They were not found in the act of breaking in, as if this were the blood of a thief caught in a crime; the guilt is of another kind, and it is charged to them.

Arminian readers take the blood in the skirts as a real social crime, the killing or oppression of the innocent poor, which they cannot explain away as lawful self-defense against burglars.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a charge of blood, the souls of the innocent poor, found on the people, and the denial that those poor were found breaking in. The injustice stands “because of all these things.” alongside the rest of the indictment.

Both traditions share the accusation. The verse adds violence against the poor to the case, and it needs no invented legal commentary beyond what the line itself says.

verses.text: “Yet you said, ‘I am innocent. Surely his anger has turned away from me.’ “Behold, I will judge you, because you say, ‘I have not sinned.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Yet they said, “I am innocent. Surely his anger has turned away from me.” The LORD answers, “Behold, I will judge you, because you say, ‘I have not sinned.’” The claim of innocence, and the claim that anger has already turned away, become themselves a reason for judgment. They say they have not sinned, and they will be judged for that saying as well as for the deeds already named.

Arminian readers hear a false peace. The people declare themselves innocent and safe, and that declaration does not make them so; it is a refusal to confess what has been charged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quoted claims as the people’s self-acquittal, which the LORD will judge. “I have not sinned” is their word, and it does not turn his anger away; it brings the judgment the verse announces.

Shared ground: the plea of innocence is false. The verse is not a contrast over the nature of justification; it is the LORD’s answer to a people who will not admit sin.

verses.text: Why do you go about so much to change your ways? You will be ashamed of Egypt also, as you were ashamed of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Why do you go about so much to change your ways? You will be ashamed of Egypt also, as you were ashamed of Assyria.” The restless changing of ways, already pictured as running to Egypt and to Assyria, will end in shame from both directions. The shame of Assyria is treated as already known; Egypt will disappoint in the same way.

Arminian readers hear a real question about this going about. The policy of shifting trusts is their own, and it will shame them again, as it has already shamed them with Assyria.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the “Why do you go about so much to change your ways?” as the LORD’s exposure of a restless seeking of help, which will lead to shame from Egypt as from Assyria.

Both traditions share the warning. The two powers are named as failed trusts, without a need to reconstruct every embassy or campaign here.

verses.text: You will also leave that place with your hands on your head; for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you won’t prosper with them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will also leave that place with your hands on your head; for the LORD has rejected those in whom you trust, and you won’t prosper with them.” Leaving with hands on the head is a gesture of grief or shame; the exact posture can be stated modestly. The reason is given: the LORD has rejected the ones they trust, and they will not prosper with them.

Arminian readers take the coming departure and the failed trust as the fruit of choosing helpers the LORD has rejected. They will not prosper with those helpers, a real outcome of a real misplaced trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same verdict: the LORD has rejected those in whom the people trust, so they will leave in shame and will not prosper with them. The close of the chapter is his rejection of the false confidences, not a small setback.

Shared ground: Egypt, or whatever “that place” is in this warning, will not be a refuge. The verse ends the unit as an indictment, not as a completed later history.
